Introduction - July 2011 











##### **Prices remain at elevated levels despite concerns about demand** 

###### **Supply side may eventually kick back in** 

We have noted previously that the key to recent price movements for the individual metals has been the earlier price performance, with those that had lagged the market earlier in the cycle holding up the best.  There is, in our view, only so long that such a trend can remain in place. 

In our previous monthly reports we have focused on the underlying view that, given the current

elevated base metal prices, a constant stream of bullish news is required to support these levels.  Our view remains that this news flow will not be maintained and we expect lower prices during the summer months. 

We believe that supply factors will once again influence relative price changes.  Nothing has changed significantly to alter our view on the supply side.  We still see structural tightness for copper and tin.  This has supported a move back towards $10,000/tonne for copper.  Despite the high copper price we see limited potential for sharply higher output given the issue of lower grades at a number key producers and the increasing reliance of future production growth from areas with extreme political and economic risk. 

As highlighted in the Economics section there are concerns about the rate of economic growth going forward.  Also there is the recognition that the inventory rebuild that helped to support the exceptionally strong demand growth in 2010 will not be such an issue in 2011. 

While economic growth rates within China remain high, we are cautious about the prospects of whether this will filter through to sharply higher demand growth.  In addition, high production growth rates for most of the base metals in China suggest that imports of base metals will slow in the coming months. 

For tin there has been a correction from elevated price levels.  However, our view on the underlying market fundamentals remains unchanged.  We still see limited gains to global production.  Capacity constraints will limit production growth in Peru, while attempts to curb “illegal mining” in Indonesia remains an issue.  Despite the high level of prices, we have only seen modest gains in Chinese output. We expect tin prices to rebound in the second half of the year. 

###### **Demand environment is easing slightly** 

Given the exceptionally high prices, both from a historical context and in relation to the marginal costs of production, the markets are always vulnerable to a correction.  We note that some of the latest data pertaining to downstream activity is starting to ease, in contrast to the environment seen in May and early June.  We view the demand side as being much weaker than in our previous reports.  Part of this reflects seasonal factors, but our view is that fundamental underlying demand has slowed. 

For lead, ongoing production problems should provide some underlying support for prices.  However, given recent gains in the lead price, we believe that further upside potential is limited.  For zinc the recent strong price has little underlying fundamental support and we expect a price correction in the third quarter.  We note the slowdown in the rate of production growth for aluminium; however we doubt whether this slowdown will lead to a significant reduction in the huge inventory overhang in the market. 

Our discussions with downstream producers confirm that demand growth is easing.  We are noting weakness in the southern European mar

ket and also slower activity in countries such as the United Kingdom and France. Despite slightly stronger underlying growth within the United States, most shipments and premium data also points to easier demand conditions. Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices

Economic Indicators - July 2011 











The United States’ construction sector remains depressed, although there have been some recent signs of improvement from the very low base.  Indeed, housing starts rose to an annualised rate of 560,000 units over the month, up 3.5% from the April pace.  The growth actually reinforces a trend toward stability and away from further deceleration in the housing construction sector, with a 49,000-unit rise in housing permit issuance from April implying that housing starts could continue to pick up in the coming months. 

China’s industrial production registered a sharp expansion of 15.3% year-on-year in June, somewhat higher than market expectations considering that monetary tightening measures were expected to weigh on growth.  On a monthly basis, the seasonall

y adjusted figure also increased by 1.5% from May’s level. Other statistics also suggest that Chinese economy remains robust, including the 9.5% GDP growth in the second quarter and the 25.6% rise in fixed asset investment over June, both on a year-on-year basis. Given China’s high inflation rates, we would not be surprised to see a further tightening of monetary policy, which would likely lead to a slow down in industrial production growth to a more sustainable pace in the second half of 2011. One area which has already shown notable signs of slowing over the start of the year has been the Chinese auto industry. Although June production of 1.49 million units rose 3.6% year-on-year, the growth represented a notable slowdown from that seen last year. In Japan, industrial production rebounded by 5.7% monthon-month in May, rising for the second consecutive month after the sharp fall in March, mainly contributed by transport equipment, general machinery and chemicals. However, on a year-ago seasonally adjusted basis, the output was still 7.2% lower than May 2010. Looking ahead, although regional power shortages are still likely to constrain industrial activity in Tokyo and surrounding areas into the peak Japanese summer demand period, easing supply chain interruptions are expected to support the rebound in production nationally and abroad in the coming months. **A1** Independent - Informed - International Aluminium - July 2011 ###### **Market background** Prices have come under some pressure in early July, slipping back below the $2,500/tonne level. This is line with our view that, despite the technical tightness, eventually the market will focus on the still 4 million tonne stick overhang. As highlighted in our supply-demand balances, we do not see the fundamental support for further gains in prices. The average price in June was $2,555/tonne, down slightly from $2,592/tonne in May, with prices back below $2,500/tonne in mid-July. As ever, there is the issue of the massive LME stockpile that is overhanging the market. We believe that the environment of higher interest rates that is emerging will lead to some of this metal being released back into the market. From a broader perspective, the massive LME stockpile is unlikely to be drawn down given the underlying fundamentals, implying that the recent outperformance of aluminium may begin to lose some momentum.
